https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4554.text: Slovak Television and Radio is opening a special exhibition to celebrate 100 years of radio broadcasting and 70 years of television broadcasting in Slovakia. The exhibition opens to the public on August 3rd at the Slovak Radio building in Bratislava and will run until November 3rd. Divided into three sections, it presents the history of Slovak radio and television, displays historic broadcasting equipment and features well-known children's characters. Visitors can also use an audio guide available in ten languages, including Romani and Rusyn. The recordings were produced by journalists from minority-language editorial teams and Radio Slovakia International without the use of artificial intelligence. According to Slovak Radio Director Peter Janků, the exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to reflect on a century of broadcasting history in the iconic inverted pyramid building. Source: STVR

Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old woman, was discovered alive on the fourth floor of her partially buried house in the Nuwakot district by Nepal's Armed Police Force on 5 September, according to Reuters. She was airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment, Reuters reported. More on this story. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Light plane plunges into Queensland paddock, sparks grass fire A light aircraft has plunged into a rural property in Queensland, sparking a fast‑moving grass fire and a massive emergency response, with grave fears held for the people on board, AAP reports. The plane went down on a paddock south of Brisbane after 11am on Monday, with shocked residents raising the alarm as smoke billowed across paddocks. Crews were called to a grass fire just after 11am and arrived to find plane debris scattered on the Chambers Flat property and flames racing through dry grass across an area about 300 by 400 metres, authorities said. At least a dozen fire trucks and multiple crews worked to contain the blaze, which burned close to a farmhouse before being brought under control about 12.50pm. No homes were damaged. Police have cordoned off the crash site and have yet to confirm how many people were on board or whether anyone has been injured. Paramedics and firefighters remain at the scene as investigator

https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2.text: 00:00:00 00:00:00 Today in Focus Russia The Pussy Riot activist turned Kremlin informer – podcast Their opposition to Putin led to two of the group being sent to brutal prison camps. Then another was found to be spying for the Kremlin. Shaun Walker reports More ways to listen Apple podcasts Spotify RSS Feed Download Presented by Helen Pidd with Shaun Walker ; produced by Ivor Manley and Rudi Zygadlo ; executive producer Homa Khaleeli Mon 28 Sep 2026 22.00 EDT Share It’s January 2012 and Pussy Riot are filming a video in Red Square, Moscow. As snow covers the cobbles and dusts the onion globes of St Basil’s Cathedral, the clock on the Kremlin chimes 11am. Eight women in colourful balaclavas leap on to a stone platform, one with an electric guitar. They start playing their latest song, Putin Has Chickened Out. It’s pretty punchy, with lyrics such as: “The rebellious column is heading to the Kremlin / Windows are exploding in FSB offices.” The group had formed a few months earlier after Vladimir Putin announced that he planned to return to the Kremlin for a third term as president. Inspired by the Arab spring the previous year, they hoped to bring revolution to Russia and stop Putin. Instead, the state cracked down hard. Three Pussy Riot members were found guilty of hooliganism after later protests, with two spending two years in some of Russia’s harshest jails. Then, in August this year, another video featuring a Pussy Riot member, Rita Flores, went viral. This time, it wasn’t a punk performance. Flores had a confession. She was an informant for the FSB, the Russian intelligence service, she said. She told the Guardian’s special correspondent Shaun Walker her story. About how her handlers threatened and cajoled her into spying on the other artists in her collective and how she tried to thwart them. Meanwhile, Helen Pidd calls Masha Alekhina , a founder member of Pussy Riot who was jailed for her support of the group and fled the country. Alekhina tells Helen about why she does not feel angry at her former comrade in activism. https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-new.text: Poland was plunged into a political crisis on Saturday, after the suspension of the country's constitutional tribunal chief escalated a battle between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's centrist government and the nationalist right for control of the judiciary.The crisis spilled onto the streets as protests erupted around the tribunal in Warsaw late Friday, with President Karol Nawrocki making a mid-air return to Poland.Poland's constitutional tribunal on Friday announced that its longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, had suspended the tribunal's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and taken charge of the court.Swieczkowski was appointed during the tenure of the previous Law and Justice party (PiS) government, which was in power from 2015 to 2023. Tusk's pro-European goverment has been seeking to reform the tribunal and remove judges appointed by the former nationalist government, arguing that the court's independence needs to be restored. The European Union has in the past accused the court of being too close to the nationalist party, specifically when PiS was in power. Also Read | A suspended chief justice, riot police, and 'coup' claims: What's happening in PolandThe suspension triggered protests, with right-wing leaders accusing Tusk's government of staging a “coup.” The escalating standoff also prompted Polish President Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, to cut short his official visit to Senegal.Suspension triggers protests, riot police deployedRiot police was deployed around the tribunal on Friday after suspension of its chief justice, even as hundreds of followers of the opposition right-wing PiS protested the ousting of Bogdan Swieczkowski.Dozens of police personnel were seen guarding the entrance to the court, according to AFP. Some of the gathered protesters chanted “Tusk traitor” as they criticised Poland's current government. One of the protesters accused Tusk of “trampling” the Polish citizens'constitutional rights, AFP reported.Some of the protesters allegedly tried to force their way through the security barricades. The cops said three protesters had been arrested for trying to enter the tribunal complex.Polish President returns, confronts Korwin-PiotrowskaPolish President Nawrocki called off his Senegal trip mid-flight. “At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning,” Nawrocki said in a post on X.Nawrocki, after returning to Warsaw, held a meeting at the presidential palace with suspended court chief Swieczkowski and the court's first chief justice Zbigniew Kapinski, according to AFP.The Polish President then entered the constitutional court building, his chief of staff Pawel Szefernaker said, adding that Nawrocki was also accompanied by Kapinski. A video of the President confronting the Donald Tusk-backed ‘head of court’ Anna Korwin-Piotrowska was shared by Russian state-backed media RT. In the video, he was reportedly heard saying, “You are not the judges of the Constitutional Court.”‘Restoring rule of law our duty’: Polish govt's responsePolish PM Tusk justified the move, saying in a post on X that “restoring the rule of law” was his government's “duty.” “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” Tusk added.Justice minister Waldemar Zurek, who is also the attorney general, told reporters that he had also requested for the lifting of the legal immunity granted to Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski. “This court has become private property; we must restore its proper functioning,” AFP cited Zurek as saying.Also Read | US envoy in Poland urges calm as constitutional tribunal crisis sparks ‘coup’ claimsKorwin-Piotrowska said the constitutional court was essential for a modern democratic state, adding that it acts as a “guarantor” of people's rights and freedoms. “In modern Europe, a democratic state cannot function without a constitutional court... that acts as a guarantor of citizens' rights and freedoms,” she said.Constitutional court's X handle alleges 'coup d'etat'The constitutional court's official handle on X, meanwhile, said there had been a “coup d'etat.” Meanwhile, the court's website, where the note announcing Swieczkowski's removal was posted, was not accessible on Friday evening.However, the court's X account said Swieczkowski remained in office, adding that Korwin-Piotrowska could not become interim chief of the tribunal, given that she had not been sworn in by the presidentPoland's long-running judiciary battleA long-running political dispute over the constitutional tribunal has crippled the institution, news agency Reuters reported. The current pro-European administration and the right-wing ally President have both refused to recognise appointees from the other side.The dispute began in 2015, when the nationalist PiS government sought to appoint judges on seats already filled by the previous government. This led to PiS nominees gaining a majority in the court, with critics saying the institution did not qualify as an impartial tribunal established by law, Reuters reported.Therefore, when Tusk's coalition came to power in 2023, it pledged to reform the court. However, Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, has attempted to block these efforts since he became President in 2025.
